KEY MESSAGE 1...The forecast continues to be very challenging and 
low confidence this evening and tonight in terms of how upstream 
convection will evolve and impact our region. Two complexes of
thunderstorms are currently ongoing. The largest and most
organized of the two complexes (MCS's) is currently propagating
S to SE across eastern Wisconsin, Lake Michigan, western Lower
Michigan, northern Illinois, and NW Indiana. This MCS has
produced widespread significant wind damage and multiple
tornadoes but will continue to make a hard right turn to the S
as it follows the eastern periphery of the thermal ridge, where
a very impressive theta e/instability gradient is draped from N
to S along a quasi-stationary front. This will allow this
MCS to largely miss our area to the west this evening, but the
eastern edge of it may clip the I-75 corridor in the roughly
21-00Z (5 to 8 PM) timeframe with gusty winds and heavy
rainfall. 

The second and smaller of the two MCS's is located
over southern Lake Huron and southern Ontario Province. This MCS
is being more directly forced by the strong mid/upper shortwave trough
that is seen on water vapor imagery digging into the northern 
Great Lakes this afternoon. As this shortwave dives through the
central Great Lakes this evening, the left exit of a 115-120
knot H3 jet streak will generate strong synoptic forcing to
sustain this MCS, as well as strengthen a surface low that will
move SE into southern Ontario tonight. Despite lower
instability across northern Ohio and NW PA (2000 MLCAPE)
compared to the extreme instability feeding the larger Lake
Michigan MCS, the combination of the jet support and surface low
should maintain this Lake Huron convection into our area.
Current trajectories time this MCS to reach NE Ohio and NW PA in
the 22 to 23Z (6 to 7 PM) timeframe. The aforementioned 
sufficient MLCAPE combined with 40-50 knots of effective deep 
layer bulk shear oriented perpendicular to the convection will 
support at least scattered severe winds, especially as the 
boundary layer continues to warm late this afternoon, with DCAPE
increasing to over 1000 J/Kg. Even in the absence of severe 
weather, most areas will see some rain and thunder with this 
activity.
 
KEY MESSAGE 2...
After a lull early tonight, additional showers and
thunderstorms are expected ahead of the cold front as the 
mid/upper jet support moves overhead tied to the shortwave
crossing the central Great Lakes. The convection this evening
should overturn the atmosphere and effectively use much of the
instability, but the aforementioned left exit region dynamics
will encourage strong forcing ahead of the cold front to get the
additional convection going overnight. This convection should
generally not be severe given the lower instability, but gusty
winds and locally heavy rainfall will be possible. Maintained
high POPS overnight until the cold front clears the area. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...
The mid/upper shortwave will become vertically stacked with the
surface low and close off over upstate New York by Tuesday
evening. This along with the parent longwave mid/upper trough
becoming negatively tilted across the eastern CONUS by Wednesday
and Thursday will allow the system to evolve into a coastal low
near Long Island. The result for northern Ohio and NW PA will 
be broad cyclonic flow and associated cold air advection Tuesday
through Thursday. A secondary front or surface trough dropping 
through the region Tuesday afternoon combined with the 
deepening trough aloft will generate scattered showers, mainly 
in interior NE Ohio and NW PA, so increased POPS Tuesday 
afternoon. Otherwise, wraparound moisture in the cyclonic flow 
combined with cold air advection across the warm lakes will lead
to periodic lake enhanced showers over far NE Ohio and NW PA 
through Wednesday before Canadian high pressure finally builds 
into the central Great Lakes and Ohio Valley late Wednesday and 
persists through the end of the week, supporting pleasantly cool
and dry conditions areawide. Low temperatures will drop into 
the 50s both Thursday and Friday mornings allowing the air 
conditioners to get a break before gradual warming over the 
weekend.
